title: What the Dangote Refinery IPO Prospectus Will Tell You (And What to Look For Before You Invest)
summary: The Dangote Refinery IPO prospectus has been submitted to the SEC for review. Here is a section-by-section guide to what it will contain, what each section means for retail investors, and the specific numbers to look for before you apply.
body_markdown:
**In short:** The Dangote Refinery IPO has been approved by the SEC, and its headline terms are confirmed: 4.1 billion shares at ₦525 each, a minimum of 10 shares, and a subscription window of 14 September to 13 October 2026. The full prospectus is not yet public. When it is published, read it for the refinery’s audited financials, its debt, the dividend terms, the use of proceeds, and the risk factors. This is general information, not advice.


The Dangote Petroleum Refinery IPO has been approved by the[Securities and Exchange Commission](https://sec.gov.ng/) , and the offer’s headline terms were confirmed at the signing ceremony on 7 September 2026. What has not yet happened is the publication of the full prospectus, the detailed legal document on which every investment decision about this offering should be based. It is expected to be made public before the subscription window opens on 14 September 2026.


That distinction matters. You now know the price, the size, and the dates. What you do not yet have is the deep detail: the refinery’s audited financials, its debt, the exact dividend mechanism, and the risk factors. All of that lives in the prospectus, and when it is published it will either confirm, modify, or correct every claim made publicly about this offering since February 2026.


This guide walks through each major section of the prospectus, explains what it will contain, and identifies the specific figures and disclosures to look for, so that the moment the document is available you know exactly where to go and what to check. It is general information, not investment advice.


## What the offer confirms so far


Ahead of the full prospectus, the SEC’s approval and the 7 September signing ceremony have already confirmed the headline terms:


- **Shares on offer:** 4,100,000,000 (4.1 billion) ordinary shares
- **Price:** ₦525.00 per share, at a fixed price
- **Minimum application:** 10 shares (₦5,250), with further applications in multiples to be set out in the prospectus
- **Subscription window:** 14 September to 13 October 2026
- **Potential size:** about ₦2.15 trillion if fully subscribed
- **Listing:** on the Main Board of the[Nigerian Exchange](https://ngxgroup.com/) after the offer closes
- **Oversubscription:** the issuer may absorb up to 30% above the offer size, subject to SEC approval


You can read plain-language summaries of these confirmed terms in our guides on[how to buy Dangote Refinery IPO shares](https://learn.investbamboo.com/how-to-buy-dangote-refinery-ipo-shares-in-nigeria-a-step-by-step-guide/) and[how much you need to invest](https://learn.investbamboo.com/how-much-do-you-need-to-invest-in-an-ipo-2/) . The full prospectus, with the audited financials and detailed disclosures, is still to come. That is the document this guide prepares you to read.


## What a prospectus is and why it matters


A prospectus is the formal legal document a company must file with the SEC and publish before it can offer shares to the public in Nigeria. It is prepared under the[Investments and Securities Act](https://sec.gov.ng/) and must be approved by the SEC before the subscription window opens, which it has been.


The prospectus differs from every other document associated with an IPO in one critical way: it is legally enforceable. If a material fact in it turns out to be false or misleading, the company and its directors can be held liable. This is why the language is careful and precise, and why you should take it more seriously than anything said in a media interview or a roadshow. For the Dangote Refinery, this prospectus will be the first time the company’s full audited financial statements, debt levels, cost structure, and operational details are made public, because the refinery has operated privately until now. If you are new to reading these documents, our general guide on[how to read an IPO prospectus](https://learn.investbamboo.com/how-to-read-an-ipo-prospectus-before-you-invest/) covers the basics.


## Section by section: what the Dangote prospectus will contain


### The cover page and summary


Every prospectus opens with a cover page stating the offering’s name, the number of shares, the offer price, the opening and closing dates, and the issuing houses and advisers. For this offer, the cover page will confirm the issuing entity, the 4.1 billion ordinary shares on offer, the fixed ₦525 price, the 10-share minimum, and the 14 September to 13 October window. It will also carry the SEC registration and approval reference confirming the document passed regulatory review. Read the summary that follows first for orientation, but do not stop there; it will not carry the detail needed for a well-informed decision.


### Business description


This section will be the company’s own account of what it does and how it makes money. For the refinery, it will cover the 650,000-barrel-per-day facility, its product mix (petrol, diesel, aviation fuel, polypropylene, fertiliser), its share of domestic fuel supply, its export operations, and its crude supply arrangements, including the relationship with NNPC, which holds a minority stake. It should also cover the expansion plan toward 1.4 million barrels per day.


**What to look for:** the specific revenue split between domestic fuel sales (naira-denominated) and export revenues (dollar-denominated). This ratio is the foundation of the dollar dividend’s credibility. A refinery earning mostly naira at home has a weaker basis for dollar dividends than one where exports dominate.


### Audited financial statements


This will be the most important section for any serious investor, and the one most commonly skipped. It typically sits toward the back, so reaching it takes deliberate effort. It will include at least three years of audited accounts: a profit and loss statement, a balance sheet, and a cash flow statement, signed off by independent auditors. Crucially, the prospectus must break out the refinery’s standalone financials, not just group-level figures, because the IPO is for the refinery entity.


**What to look for:** revenue in both naira and dollar terms and its growth; EBITDA and operating profit, heavily influenced by the crack spread between crude input costs and product prices; net profit and earnings per share, which is what dividends are paid from; free cash flow, the cash left after capital expenditure and debt service, which determines near-term dividend capacity; and the interest coverage ratio (operating profit divided by interest expense), where a figure below two is a warning that debt is consuming too much of earnings.


### Capitalisation and debt structure


This section will disclose total borrowings, the currencies of the debt, interest rates, maturities, and any covenants. The refinery cost around $20 billion to build, financed through a mix of equity, development finance loans, and commercial credit, and the prospectus will reveal how much remains outstanding and on what terms. Check in particular whether any facilities have change-of-control clauses triggered by the IPO, which could direct part of the proceeds to debt repayment rather than growth.


**What to look for:** the total debt to EBITDA ratio, where above four is high leverage for a cyclical industrial company, and net debt (borrowings minus cash) as the more precise measure. Note the credit-rating context too and whether any rating applies to the refinery entity specifically.


### Use of proceeds


This will tell you exactly what the company intends to do with the money raised, and it is one of the most important sections for judging alignment between the company’s ambitions and what you are funding. The proceeds have been publicly linked to expansion toward 1.4 million barrels per day and wider group investments. Broad statements like “general corporate purposes” are insufficient and deserve scrutiny.


**What to look for:** a specific, itemised breakdown of how proceeds will be deployed, with timelines, and whether any portion goes to debt repayment rather than growth. There is nothing wrong with reducing leverage, but you should know whether you are funding expansion, balance-sheet repair, or both.


### Dividend policy


Given the proposed dollar dividend structure, this will be among the most closely read sections. It will disclose how dividends are declared and paid, the frequency, the payout basis, and the currencies of settlement. If the dollar dividend arrangement has final regulatory approval, this section will confirm who qualifies, how the currency election is made, the mechanism for converting export revenues into dollar payments, and when the option could be suspended. If it is still conditional, the section will state what is confirmed and what remains subject to clearance.


**What to look for:** whether the dollar dividend is confirmed or conditional; if conditional, what must happen for it to take effect and by when; the expected payout ratio; and whether there is any minimum dividend commitment or whether payments are entirely at the board’s discretion.


### Risk factors


Every Nigerian prospectus contains a dedicated risk factors section, and it is the closest thing to unvarnished honesty the document holds, because failing to disclose a material risk creates legal liability. Pay attention to how the company describes the dollar dividend regulatory risk, crude supply security, the expansion plan’s execution risk, and the relationship between naira volatility and its cost structure.


**What to look for:** risks described in vague, hedged language rather than specific, quantified terms. “The company may be affected by commodity price fluctuations” is far less useful than a disclosure that quantifies the impact of a specific fall in crack spreads. Quantified risk disclosure is a sign of a well-prepared prospectus.


### Directors, management, and corporate governance


This will list the board, senior management, and governance structure, and disclose material transactions between the company and its directors or major shareholders. That is especially relevant here, because the majority shareholder controls multiple affiliated businesses with commercial relationships to the refinery.


**What to look for:** related-party transactions. Any arrangement between the refinery and other group entities, such as crude procurement or service contracts, should be disclosed on arm’s length terms. If the refinery pays above-market prices to affiliates, that directly reduces profitability.


### Material contracts


This will disclose contracts material to operations, including crude supply agreements, offtake agreements, loan facilities, and joint ventures. For the refinery, look at the NNPC crude supply arrangement, any export offtake agreements, and the terms of remaining major debt facilities.


**What to look for:** whether the crude supply arrangement is fixed or market-linked, the duration of key offtake agreements, and whether the commercial relationships underpinning the investment case are locked into long-term contracts or run on a short-term basis.


## The five most important numbers to find


Once the document is published, locate these first:


1. **Refinery-level EBITDA** , not group-level. The IPO valuation is for the refinery, so assess the multiple against the refinery’s own earnings.
2. **Total net debt** , the difference between borrowings and cash, which tells you how much of the enterprise value belongs to lenders versus shareholders.
3. **Dollar revenue as a percentage of total revenue** , which determines the credibility of the dollar dividend and the company’s exposure to naira depreciation.
4. **Interest coverage ratio** , which shows how much cushion exists between earnings and debt obligations.
5. **The confirmed dollar dividend mechanism** , whether approved, conditional, or pending, and what the operational path to receiving dollars actually looks like.


## What strong signals look like


A prospectus from a company genuinely ready for public markets tends to show several things: audited financials from a well-regarded accounting firm; specific, quantified risk disclosures rather than vague ones; a clear, itemised use of proceeds mapping capital to named projects with timelines; and straightforward related-party disclosures describing arm’s length terms and board approval. These signal a governance culture consistent with public company standards.


## What red flags look like


Conversely, watch for overly broad risk language that describes risks without quantifying them; a use of proceeds section dominated by “general corporate purposes”; related-party transactions described vaguely without independent confirmation of arm’s length pricing; a sharp, unexplained jump in profitability just ahead of the IPO; significant debt maturing within one to two years of listing; and dividend language tying all payments to board discretion with no minimum or forward guidance. None of these alone is a reason to avoid the offer. Each is a reason to ask a sharper question and look for a specific answer before committing.


## How to access the prospectus when it is published


When the approved prospectus is published, it will be available through official channels: the[NGX Group website](https://ngxgroup.com/) , the SEC Nigeria website, the Dangote Group’s corporate communications, and through the Bamboo app once the offer goes live on the platform. Do not rely on third-party summaries, including from media outlets or investment platforms, as a substitute for reading the actual document. Summaries orient you; the prospectus is the basis for the decision.


The most efficient way to read it will be to start with the summary, then go to the audited financial statements and the capitalisation and debt section, then the dividend policy, then the risk factors, and finally the use of proceeds. That sequence covers the five critical numbers and the most important qualitative disclosures in the right order.


## Frequently asked questions


**Has the Dangote Refinery prospectus been published?** The offer has been approved by the SEC and its headline terms were confirmed at the signing ceremony on 7 September 2026, but the full prospectus document has not yet been made publicly available. It is expected to be published before or as the subscription window opens on 14 September 2026.


**What has already been confirmed?** The offer of 4.1 billion ordinary shares at a fixed ₦525 per share, a minimum application of 10 shares, the 14 September to 13 October subscription window, a potential raise of about ₦2.15 trillion, and a listing on the NGX Main Board. The detailed financials, debt, and dividend mechanism will come in the full prospectus.


**What is the most important thing to look for in it?** The refinery’s standalone audited financials, especially EBITDA and the split between naira and dollar revenue; the total net debt; and the confirmed terms of the dollar dividend arrangement.


**Is the dollar dividend confirmed?** The dollar dividend has been announced, and the prospectus will set out its status and exact terms. Read the dividend policy section to see whether it is fully approved or conditional, and on what.


**Where will I be able to read the prospectus?** Through the NGX Group website, the SEC Nigeria website, the Dangote Group’s corporate communications, and the Bamboo app once the offer goes live.[Download Bamboo here](https://onelink.to/investbamboo) to be ready when it is published.


**Do I need to read the whole prospectus before investing?** Not every page, but the audited financial statements, capitalisation and debt, dividend policy, risk factors, and use of proceeds sections are not optional reading for anyone putting meaningful capital into the offer.
